4.9.m: Sūta said: 'Then those hosts of immortals, along with the gandharvas and dānavas, / uprooted Mount Mandara and cast it into the reservoir of waters.
Then the eternal, glorious, compassionate Lord of the universe / held the base of the mountain upon his back in the form of a tortoise.
Wrapping Ananta around it, they churned the ocean of milk; / as it was being churned on the eleventh day, there first arose, O twice-born,
the Kālakūṭa poison; seeing it, they all fled away. / Then, seeing them fleeing, Śaṅkara spoke these words:
'O hosts of immortals, do not regard this poison with fear; / I will quickly avert the great Kālakūṭa poison.'
Having spoken thus, the lord of Pārvatī, meditating on Nārāyaṇa in his heart / and uttering the great mantra, took the dreadful poison.
By the power of the great mantra, that mighty poison was digested. / "Acyuta, Ananta, Govinda"—these three names of Hari,
whoever carefully mutters with devotion, beginning with the praṇava and ending with "namaḥ", / for him there is no fear born of poison, snakebite, or fire, nor any fear of death.
Then, their minds delighted, the gods churned the Ocean of Milk. / Then arose Alakṣmī, black-faced and red-eyed,
with rough, tawny hair, bearing the body of an old woman. / And that elder sister said to the gods: 'What is to be done by me?'
The gods then spoke to that goddess who is the vessel of sorrow: / 'In the houses of those mortals where strife prevails, O goddess,
there we assign your abode; dwell there, O elder sister, auspiciously. / And those men who speak harsh words, and who tell lies,
and who eat at the twilights, dwell in their houses, O giver of sorrow! / Where there are skulls, hair, ashes, bones, chaff, and burning coals,
there, O elder sister, will be your abode, without a doubt. / And the vile men who eat without having washed their two feet,
always dwell in their house, O giver of sorrow and poverty! / Those who clean their teeth with sand, salt, and charcoal,
always dwell in their house, O giver of sorrow, along with Kali! / Those vile men who eat mushrooms and remnants of the wood-apple,
in their home is your dwelling, O elder sister, O giver of defilement! / Those who eat sesamum paste, bottle gourd, carrot, spinach leaves,
water spinach, and onion, those evil-minded people— / in their house will be your dwelling, without a doubt.
Where there is no worship of gurus, gods, and guests, and no sacrifice or charitable gift, / where there is no sound of the Veda, dwell there always, O inauspicious one!
Where there is strife between husband and wife, where ancestors and gods are not worshiped, / where they are addicted to gambling, dwell there always, O inauspicious one!

Where men are attached to the wives of others, where they steal others' property, / where there is no reverence for brāhmaṇas, virtuous men, and the elderly, / dwell always in that place, O giver of sin and poverty!'
Having thus instructed the eldest [sister] of the gods, the favorite of Kali among all, / they, with focused minds, churned the milk ocean again.

4.10.m: Sūta said: 'Then Airāvata was born, and likewise the horse Uccaiḥśravas, / Dhanvantari, the Pārijāta tree, Surabhi, and the hosts of apsarases.
Then, at dawn on the twelfth day when the sun had risen, / Mahālakṣmī arose, the glorious one, adorned with all auspicious marks.
The righteous gods saw that great goddess, the mother / of all beings, joyful, whose dwelling is the heart of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Then the cool-rayed moon, the brother of Lakṣmī, was born along with the nectar; / and Tulasī was born, the purifier of the worlds, the wife of Hari.
Having placed that mountain back as before, their desires fulfilled, / gathering together and praising the Mother, they muttered the supreme Śrīsūkta.
Then that goddess, being pleased, said to all the gods: / 'Choose a boon; may it be well with you! I am a giver of boons, O best of the gods!'
The gods said: 'Be gracious, O Kamalā, O goddess, Mother of all, beloved of Hari! / Without you, the world is desolate; protect our lives!'
Addressed thus, that Mahālakṣmī, beloved of Nārāyaṇa, said: / "Now I shall protect the lives of all living beings."
Then the glorious Nārāyaṇa, holding the conch, discus, and mace, / suddenly appeared, the compassionate Lord of the universe.
Then those gods praised him, bowing down to the Lord of the worlds; / with folded hands, speaking in voices choked with joy, they said:
'Accept the Mother, O Viṣṇu, your beloved consort, / never-departing Lakṣmī, for the protection of worldly existence.' / Before he could make his promise, Indirā spoke to Hari:

Lakṣmī said: 'Without having married off the elder sister Alakṣmī, O Madhusūdana, / how do you wish to marry me, her younger sister, O Lord? / For when an elder sister is present, the younger sister should not be wed.'
Sūta said: 'Hearing this, Viṣṇu then gave Alakṣmī to Uddālaka / in accordance with the Vedic precept, along with the gods.'
Then glorious Nārāyaṇa accepted Lakṣmī; / thereupon all the hosts of gods bowed down again and again.
Then, superior in strength, they struck down all the asuras; / and screaming, they all fled in the ten directions.
The gods formed a row in due order to consume the nectar; / by order of glorious Viṣṇu, they all spoke among one another.
They said, "Give to yourself, give to yourself, give to yourself!" / and they said, "I am unable, I am unable, I am unable!"
Then Viṣṇu arose and assumed the form of a woman; / he served that nectar from a golden vessel.
As soon as Rāhu consumed the nectar, O best of twice-borns, / the moon and sun spoke: "This is a rākṣasa who has arrived by deceit!"
Then the enraged Lord of the Universe struck [him] with the golden vessel; / his head fell to the earth, and he came to be known by the name of Ketu.
Then Rāhu and Ketu quickly departed, both agitated with fear; / now, whenever that day arrives, he fights with the moon and sun.
The son of Siṃhikā causes an eclipse; that moment is very rare to attain. / All water becomes equal to the Gaṅgā, and twice-borns equal to Vedavyāsa.
Whoever bathes in any sacred ford obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā; / giving becomes an imperishable merit, as if acquired through a crore of births.
Sin is destroyed along with its root—what need to speak of a crore of sacrifices? / One desiring knowledge attains knowledge; one desiring a son obtains a son;
One desiring liberation attains liberation, and mastery of mantras surely comes about. / Thus has been narrated to you, O brāhmaṇa, the churning of the ocean.

4.11.m: Śaunaka said: / Now I desire to hear; relate it truthfully, / O you instructed directly by Vedavyāsa, the embodiment of Hari!
O Sūta, free from egoism, who bestow favor upon the worlds: / By what does a woman become fortunate, and a sinful woman very unfortunate?
By what does she become dear in body to her husband, an embodiment of nectar to his eyes? / Or by what is fortune brought forth? Tell me that, O rich in asceticism!
Sūta said: / If this holy deed is extremely rare [to know], O brāhmaṇa, / listen, sir; I shall narrate it in brief and in proper order.
There was a king named Bhadraśravas in the cosmic age known as the Dvāpara age, / a resident of the country of Saurāṣṭra, thoroughly learned in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.
He had a wife born under the name Suraticandrikā; / by her, the glorious king had seven handsome sons.
Then a beautiful daughter, truthful in speech, was born, / named Śyāmabālā, O chief of brāhmaṇas, bringing joy to her father.
Then, one day, Śyāmabālā, along with her friends, in golden sands, / [seeking] to play joyfully with concealed, charming gems,
went to the base of an exceptionally rare kadamba tree. / In the meantime, O brāhmaṇa, Lakṣmī, who delivers one from worldly existence,
who bestows moral conduct upon people, came forward in person, / having assumed the form of an elderly brāhmaṇa woman, O earthly god.
[She thought:] "Without the house of the king who rules all people, / into the home of what lowlier persons shall I now go?"
Thinking thus in her mind, she went to the king's dwelling, / which was endowed with golden walls and adorned with banners.
Passing through the lion gate, she then said to the female doorkeeper: / "Open the door, O door-keeper appointed here, endowed with auspicious marks!
Let me go swiftly to see Queen Suraticandrikā." / Hearing that speech of hers, which was uttered like the voice of a cuckoo, / that woman holding a jeweled staff experienced supreme joy.

The doorkeeper said: / "What name do you bear, O old woman? And who is your husband? / Why have you come? What business do you have in seeing the queen? / Wherefore and why? Tell me, O brāhmaṇa woman, for I have great curiosity to hear!"
The old woman said: / "Listen, O ward, staff-bearer of the great king's wife, / since you have a curiosity to hear the reason for my arrival:
I am well known by the name Kamalā, and the lord of my life / is famous as Bhuvaneśa; there is a city named Dvāravatī.
In that [city] indeed my lord of life dwells, O ward; from there / have I come, O holder of the jeweled reed; hear with curiosity!
Now I will state before you the business of my arrival: / Formerly, your queen was born of a vaiśya family, and was distressed.
One day, O ward, a quarrel was started by her husband; / by that woman, distressed and afflicted by her husband,
going swiftly out of the house, crying again and again— / hearing her weeping, I came to her side.
I asked about the whole affair, and it was told truthfully / by her; thereupon I imparted instruction on an excellent vow.
From my instruction, she indeed joyfully performed that excellent vow; / by its favor, O female doorkeeper, she became happy.
At some time, the woman born of the vaiśya family fell under the power of death along with her husband. / Then, in order to fetch the two, who had committed all destructive deeds,
the lord Dharmarāja sent his servants, Caṇḍa and others. / By Yama's order the terrifying messengers of Yama arrived.
Having bound them with a leather noose, holding iron mallets in their hands, / they made ready to go toward the shelter of Yama.
In the meantime, the messengers of Lakṣmī, devoted to Viṣṇu, / bearing the conch, discus, and mace, arrived to fetch them.
Seeing them of such appearance, the messengers of Yama fled. / The noble messengers of Lakṣmī, self-luminous and radiant,
severed the noose, placed them upon a chariot yoked with royal swans, / and all swiftly went to the city of Lakṣmī along the skyey path.
For as many times as that vaiśya woman had performed that excellent vow, / for that many thousands of kalpas they both dwelt in the city of Kamalā.

Now, to experience the remainder of their merit, they are born into a royal lineage; / and proud of royal fortune, O female doorkeeper, they have forgotten the vow. / Therefore, I have come to instruct her, as well as you."
The female doorkeeper said: / "By what procedure indeed, O old woman, was this excellent vow performed? / In which month is this best of vows [performed], and which deity is worshipped?
You ought to tell this properly to me who ask, O mother!" / Kamalā said: / "When Kārttika has passed and Mārgaśīrṣa has arrived, / in that month, O ward, on the day known as Guru's day [Thursday],
then, at the morning hour, surrounded by all who keep the vow, / one should worship Lakṣmī along with Nārāyaṇa.
With sweet things, accompanied by milk-rice, and with food mixed with sugar candy, / one should please Lakṣmī, O maiden; then one should make this prayer:
"O goddess worshipped in the three worlds, O Kamalā, O beloved of Viṣṇu! / Just as you are unmoving in Kṛṣṇa, so remain dwelling in me!
O sovereign Kamalā, O sinless goddess, be my refuge!" / Having presented various articles of offering, one should please Lakṣmī.
One should worship the goddess in accordance with the scriptures, accompanied by a great festival; / then, having given the remnants of the food offering to the best of brāhmaṇas,
[one should feed] oneself, one's husband, one's sons, O ward, and also the other servants. / Now hear the specific rule for the second Thursday, O beautiful woman!
And with cakes baked [on pans] made of wheat, praised with diverse powders, / one should satisfy the goddess Kamalā, performing it indeed with a devotional disposition.
On the third [Thursday], an offering of curd-rice mixed with sugar candy [is made]; / on the fourth, one should worship with joy using the essence of śāmāka and śāli grains.
Goddess Lakṣmī [should be worshipped] with effort, holding a jewelled staff in her hand; / then, for the pleasure of Goddess Lakṣmī, one should honor brāhmaṇas with wealth,
as well as with clothes, ornaments, foods, and various kinds of fruits.” / The foster daughter said: “Stay right here, O old woman! Having informed the queen, Suraticandrikā,
I will bring you. Do not be angry, O best of women!” / Having spoken thus, that lovely-limbed woman went into the presence of the queen.
Placing her folded palms upon her head, O brāhmaṇa, the foster daughter, / starting completely from the beginning down to the full details, whatever was spoken by Kamalālayā,
recounted all that to Queen Suraticandrikā. / Hearing the words of the female gatekeeper, Queen Suraticandrikā,
the proud beauty, went to the side of the brāhmaṇa woman and spoke. / The queen said: “O old brāhmaṇa woman, what has happened? Have you come to give instruction?
Speak to me at your leisure, casting aside fear, at your ease.” / The brāhmaṇa woman said: “Having seen your injustice, I, who am fickle, wish to depart.
Why should I describe the most rare vow to an evil woman? / And today, on Indirā's day, you associate with an outcaste!
That was seen by me. What evil woman [stays] in her house now that she is haughty?” / Hearing those words of the brāhmaṇa woman, her eyes reddened with rage,
she struck that old brāhmaṇa woman. / Then she, the aged Kamalā, fled weeping.
Then the girl Śyāmā, who was playing, heard the sound of the brāhmaṇa woman weeping; / the young girl rich in austerity came into her presence.
The young girl Śyāmā said: “O old woman, who gave you such torment? Tell me!” / Hearing her words, with a voice choked with grief,
Kamalā told the whole matter, O best of the twice-born. / Then the young girl Śyāmā, having heard of the most rare vow,
performed it with faith and devotion according to the injunctions declared in the scriptures. / When three times had been completed, and the fourth day arrived,
her marriage ceremony was accomplished, O twice-born, by the favor of Lakṣmī. / Of King Śrīsiddheśvaradeva, endowed with great splendor,
a son named Mālīdhara took her and went home. / Now, when she had departed, O brāhmaṇa, hear a wonder:
All the very abundant goods that were in the queen's house / were taken away by someone; it was not known by whom, O earthly god.
She was left without wealth, bereft of sense, and lacking food and clothing. / Dejected, she sent her husband to go to their daughter's house
for the purpose of begging a little something. / After some time, O vipra, he arrived with great difficulty
at that village of Mālīdhara, on the bank of a lake. / Her female servants came there to draw water; / seeing him, foremost among the wretched, they asked, moved by pity.
The female servants said: “Who are you? From where have you arrived, devoid of flesh and blood, / with emaciated body and dry hair? Tell us all that!”
The poor man said: “I am the father of the young girl Śyāmā, arrived from the city of Saurāṣṭra. / Tell this, O maids, in the presence of the young girl Śyāmā.”
Hearing his speech, filled with curiosity, / looking at each other's faces, they all laughed and went to their city.
All the news was related to the young girl Śyāmā, O twice-born. / Hearing their words, that beautiful woman sent servants,
giving flower-oil, divine garments, sandalwood, a betel roll, / and a horse, to meet her father.
All those servants went, dressed him in excellent attire, / and led him to the house of the young girl Śyāmā, which resembled the abode of the king of gods.
Then the young girl Śyāmā diligently fed her father, / the foremost among the afflicted, with śāli-rice mixed with ghee.
When four days had passed, O one rich in austerity, / she sent him away, having given him wealth placed in a hidden vessel.
Then, having entered his own house, he saw the wealth situated inside the vessel / had become a heap of charcoal; being exceedingly grieved, he wept.
He came out of his house and went to his daughter's dwelling; / then the wretched woman [the mother] also arrived right at the shore of the lake.
When she was brought in, just as she was dear to her life, / even so the devoted wife honored her out of love for her mother.
At this time, O vipra, the young girl Śyāmā / set her mind on making her mother perform the excellent day of Lakṣmī.
Her mother, who had eaten miserable leftovers of infants / even in solitude, was visited by the wrath of Lakṣmī.
Even when the third day of Indirā had passed, / on the fourth day she firmly made her perform it.
She, Queen Suraticandrikā, went back to the city / after seeing her divine home, restored by the grace of Indirā.
And once upon a time, O chief of vipras, the young girl Śyāmā / went to her mother's house with the desire to see her prosperity.
Then, seeing the young girl Śyāmā from afar, she became enraged: / “I will not look upon her face!” saying which, she stood watching [haughtily].
Going inside the house and taking rock-salt, / she returned to her own house, keeping silent and taking refuge in Lakṣmī.
Her lord, the king, questioned that chaste woman who held her husband as her deity: / “What has been brought by you, my beloved? Tell me before anything else!”
The beloved said: “The essence of the kingdom has been brought; I will show it at the meal.” / Having said this, she then prepared the cooking without salt,
and then gave the food and other dishes to King Mālīdhara. / Then King Mālīdhara, having eaten the dish lacking salt,
experienced its tastelessness, and then she gave him the essence of the kingdom. / Then the king, delighted in mind, took his meal, O twice-born,
and praised that woman, saying, “Blessed, blessed are you!” / Any woman who does not perform this vow with great reverence
becomes poor and unfortunate birth after birth. / The woman who hears this with devotion, or the man who recites it with concentrated mind,
is freed from all sins and attains the world of Lakṣmī. / If one performs the vow without having heard this story of the vow, / the fruit of her vow is surely destroyed; there is no doubt.

4.12.m: Śaunaka said: “By what other merit, O Sūta, with his sins removed, / does a man go to the abode of Hari? Tell that out of compassion.”
Sūta said: “The mortal who protects a brāhmaṇa's life with wealth, / or with his own life, O best of the twice-born, goes to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Formerly, in the age called Dvāpara, there was a king named Dīnanātha; / he was childless, powerful, a Vaiṣṇava, and a performer of sacrifices.
Once the king, endowed with humility, questioned Gālava: / ‘By what merit may a son be born, O ocean of mercy?
Tell me, O tiger among sages; I will do it at your command. / For those men who have no son, life is indeed meaningless.’
Gālava said: ‘O King, listen attentively as I am questioned before you; / I will tell you in brief the cause of the birth of a son.’”
"Perform the sacrifice named Naramedha, best of kings; / then you will indeed have offspring endowed with all auspicious marks."

The king said:
"The Naramedha is a great sacrifice, foremost among sacrifices, O twice-born one. / What sort of man should I bring and perform [it with]? Tell me, O teacher."

Gālava said:
"He should have handsome limbs, a pleasant face, and be versed in all the scriptures; / if he is born in a good family, he is then fit for the sacrifice.

One who is deformed in limb, dark-complexioned, or foolish is certainly not fit."
When Gālava had spoken thus, O brāhmaṇa, that king, ruler of men,
sent messengers after recounting the sage's words, / and gave abundant wealth to the twice-born led by Gālava.
He selected for the sacrifice those who had reached the further shore of all scriptures. / Then, by the king's command, the messengers went gladly to country after country,
from village to village, O best of the twice-born, and into cities, intently searching; / they found no [such person] anywhere, and then went to a countryside,
to [a town] named Daśapura, O brāhmaṇa, crowded with virtuous twice-born men, / where women had lovely hair and eyes like young fawns,
and seeing whom men were infatuated, as they had moon-like faces. / In that delightful city lived a twice-born named Kṛṣṇadeva
along with his three sons and his well-behaved wife; / he was a Vaiṣṇava, pleasant-spoken, and always devoted to Viṣṇu's worship,
maintaining the sacred fires, devoted to his ancestors, and doing what is pleasing to Vaiṣṇavas. / Then those messengers of the king made an entreaty to that best of the twice-born:
"Give a son, give! Speak, O best of brāhmaṇas; / the king has no son, O best of the twice-born, who can dispel his anguish.
For that purpose, he has become initiated into the sacrifice named Naramedha. / We shall indeed take your son to offer him as a victim in the great sacrifice.
Accept four hundred thousand gold pieces, O brāhmaṇa, with an untroubled mind. / If you will not give him willingly due to longing for a son,

then we shall take him by force, for we carry out the king's command."
Hearing the messengers' words, both the brāhmaṇa and his wife were overwhelmed with grief,
and became like lifeless beings, their minds in doubt: / "What use is wealth, gold, life, or even a home?" / That brāhmaṇa also spoke these words to the royal servants.

The brāhmaṇa said:
"If you messengers have surely come to fetch my son, the dispeller of the darkness of grief, / then listen to my words.
Who living on the earth wishes to disregard the king's command? / But leave the son and take me, an old twice-born man."
Hearing his words, the messengers, filled with anger, / forcibly abandoned the gold in his house.
When they resolved in anger to carry off his son, / that twice-born man, folding his hands and weeping, said:
"Leave my eldest of sons and take another excellent son"— / this word does not come to my mouth to speak, O people!"
Hearing the twice-born's words, and seeing the virtuous brāhmaṇa's wife weeping, / the messengers said, "Give the youngest son, O best of men!"
Hearing their words, the brāhmaṇa's wife then fell / to the ground, extremely distressed, like a plantain tree before a whirlwind.
Taking up a club, she struck her own head with force: / "O messengers, I will never, under any circumstances, give my youngest son!"
At this moment, O brāhmaṇa, the middle son of the twice-born, / filled with humility, bowed to his parents and weeping said:
"If a mother should give poison, or a father sell his son, / or a king seize everything, who could be a protector then?"
Having spoken thus, his son, having bowed with his head to his father, / went swiftly with the messengers to this consecrated king.
Then the two brāhmaṇas, their minds anguished by separation from their son, / wept and wept, and went completely blind.
Then, as they were travelling along the path, / they came indeed upon the hermitage of sage Viśvāmitra, accompanied by pupils and frequented by fawn fawns.
Seeing the royal servants, that sage asked respectfully: / "Who are you? Where have you gone? State what your business is."

The king's messengers said:
"Listen attentively, O twice-born one. No son is born to the king; / for that purpose, the king is well-initiated into the sacrifice named Naramedha.

We are taking this brāhmaṇa's young son there for a sacrificial victim."
Hearing their words, that twice-born man became full of compassion:
"Let my own life-breaths depart, but let the boy be happy! / For those people in this world who, for the sake of a child, a twice-born, or a master,

abandon their lives like blades of grass, eternal worlds are theirs."
Reflecting thus in his heart, that bull among the twice-born said:
"To take a victim for the sacrifice, leave this brāhmaṇa boy / and take me quickly instead, for this boy is excellent.
Having obtained birth in worldly existence, no happiness has been attained here / by this boy; how then should he die?
Since he came from their home, O messengers, his distressed parents, / bereft of fortune, have surely gone as if to the abode of Yama."
Hearing his words in this manner, the messengers then said to the twice-born: / "Without the order of the king, the lord of the distressed, O earthly god,

how could we take you, an old and wise man?"
Having spoken thus, the messengers then went to the king's city.
That sage went to the sacrificial hall along with the company of messengers. / The messengers recounted the twice-born's conduct to the king.
Hearing that, his mind apprehensive, he spoke these words to the good [sage]: / "O sage, even if a son will be born to me once the sacrifice is performed
even without a victim, O brāhmaṇa, then take the twice-born's son."

The sage said:
"When the sacrifice has been performed by you, O king, an illustrious son will be born. / Have no doubt on this point, for the sight of me is never in vain."
Hearing his words, the king, exceedingly delighted, / made the final oblation in the sacrifice together with all the sages.
Thereupon that best of sages took the son of the brāhmaṇa / and went then to the city named Daśapura.
Having gone to his dwelling, the sage said: / "O twice-born, you stay in the house!" [The brāhmaṇa replied:] "I remain like a dead man, O sage.
The king has taken my son by force; what shall I do? / And when our son departed, O twice-born, of both of us, husband and wife,

the eyes went completely blind from crying."
Then that tiger among sages said, "Look, take your son!"
When he spoke thus, O brāhmaṇa, both the brāhmaṇas, filled with joy, / making a call for their son, came outside in an instant.
By virtue of the truth of the sage's words, that very moment their eyes / quickly regained sight, even by seeing their son.
Drinking in the lotus-face of their son with their eyes resembling black bees, / and having bowed again and again to that sage for a long time,
both those brāhmaṇas, speaking pleasantly, said these words, O twice-born: / "Oh sage, the gift of life [to our son] is indeed a meritorious deed for us both!"
Hearing the words of the two, that sage, an ocean of compassion, / gave them a blessing, O twice-born, and went to his own hermitage.
Having brought Viṣṇu's supreme abode into the palm of his hand, / that highly fortunate sage performed asceticism difficult to attain even by deities.

After some time had passed, O brāhmaṇa, a son was born to that king, / handsome and worthy of kingship, like the moon in the ocean of milk; / and at the feast celebrating his son, that king gave away wealth, O twice-born.

Free from sorrow, his curiosity aroused, he enjoyed himself like a god upon the earth.
He who protects the brahmins, even offering his life and wealth,

goes to Viṣṇu's abode, from which return is hard to attain.
Those who read here with devotion and hear the story from a brahmin,
even a single narrative or a single verse, go to the abode of Viṣṇu.

4.13.m:
Sūta said:
O brahmin, the person who observes Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī with devotion,
in the end goes to the city of Viṣṇu, accompanied by ten million generations of his family, O twice-born.

The eighth day falling on a Wednesday or a Monday, O best of the twice-born,
and joined with the constellation Rohiṇī, grants liberation to ten million generations of one's lineage.

Even if laden with great sins, if one performs this supreme vow,
he is freed from all sins, and in the end he goes to the home of Hari.

O brahmin, the lowest of men who does not observe Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī
attains misery in this world, and after death goes to hell.

And whatever foolish woman does not observe the vow of Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī
year after year, goes to a terrible hell.

The man of utterly bewildered intellect who eats food on the day of Janmāṣṭamī
feeds on a great hell; truly, truly do I say [this].

Formerly, Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages, was questioned by Dilīpa.
Hear that, O highly wise one, which destroys all sins.

Dilīpa said:
I wish to hear about the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Bhādra, on which Janārdana was born.
Tell [me], O great sage!

How was the Lord, bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, born?
Why and for what reason did Viṣṇu [enter] the womb of Devakī?

Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O king, I shall tell you why Janārdana was born
on earth, leaving heaven behind; I shall narrate it to you.

Formerly, the earth was indeed tormented by kings like Kaṃsa,
beaten by Kaṃsa’s messenger intoxicated by his own authority.

Weeping and crying out, her eyes rolling, she went
where the Lord of gods, the lover of Umā whose banner is the bull, dwells,

to report to him: “O Lord, I have been beaten by Kaṃsa!”
Raining streams of tears, pale and insulted,

seeing her crying, with his lower lip trembling with anger,
accompanied by Umā and followed by all the host of gods,

Mahādeva came in wrath to the abode of the Creator.
Having arrived, he spoke to Brahmā for the destruction of Kaṃsa:

“O Brahmā, an expedient must be devised by you together with Viṣṇu.”
Having heard that speech of the Lord, the self-born [Brahmā] resolved to go

to the Ocean of Milk, where Vaikuṇṭha sleeps upon the serpent.
Mounting the back of a swan, he went into the presence of Hari.

Arriving there, the Creator, joined with the host of gods led by Hara,
the best of those who know eloquence, praised him with tender words:

“Salutation to the lotus-eyed Hari, the supreme self!
And to the protector of the universe, the beloved of Lakṣmī, salutation be to you!”
Hearing this praise from them, Janārdana replied / to all the gods whose faces were distressed: "How have you come?"

Intoxicated by the boon given by the Trident-bearer, King Kaṃsa is unassailable.
The earth has been struck by him, afflicted by blows of his hand.

‘Though a boon was given earlier, moreover, he was deceived by delusion:
O Śambhu, my death will not be caused by anyone except my nephew.’

Therefore, O Lord, go yourself to slay the unassailable Kaṃsa,
taking birth in Devakī's womb, and going to Gokula.

Urged by Brahmā, the god replied to the Trident-bearer:
“O Lord of gods, grant Pārvatī! Having stayed [there] for a year, she will return.”

Together with Umā for protection, the bearer of conch, discus, and mace,
and the lotus-seated [Brahmā], set out towards Mathurā.

There, the wielder of the mace took birth in Devakī's womb,
while deer-eyed Śarvāṇī took up residence inside Yaśodā's belly.

After dwelling for nine months and ending with nine days in the womb,
in the month of Bhādra, in the dark fortnight, on the lunar day called Aṣṭamī,

under the constellation Rohiṇī, in a night resounding with rain-clouds,
there was born the Lord of the universe, the enemy of Kaṃsa, the son of Vasudeva.

And Yaśodā, daughter of Virāṭa and wife of Nanda, gave birth to a daughter.
[Seeing] the son holding a lotus in hand, lotus-naveled, with eyes like lotus petals,

Ānakadundubhi then began to rejoice upon seeing [him].
Terrified by fear of the demon Kaṃsa, Devakī then said:

“O lord, go indeed to the daughter of Virāṭa and deliver the son!
Having given the son to Yaśodā, bring her daughter back.”

Hearing her words, Vasudeva also became distressed;
taking the boy in his lap, he set out towards the daughter of Virāṭa.

Midway on that path was the Yamunā, filled with water,
terrible, very wide, and possessing a deep flood of water.

Seeing it thus, standing on the bank and looking at the Yamunā,
Vasudeva, afflicted with sorrow, lamented with intense anxiety:

“What shall I do? Where shall I go, deceived indeed by fate?
How shall I go here to the daughter of Virāṭa, to the house of Nanda?”

There, the father was happily deluded by Hari through his illusory power.
Having stood on the bank for only a moment, gazing at the Yamunā,

it was seen by him again to have become knee-deep in an instant.
Rejoicing at the sight of it, he stood up and began to depart.

Exercising his illusory power, the Lord of the universe fell from his father's lap into the water.
Seeing his son fallen, he cried out in great distress, “Alas, alas!”

Deceived by that fate so as to devise a great expedient once more,
[he prayed:] “Save me, O Lord of the worlds! Protect the son, O best of the gods!”

Seeing the weeping of his father, the enemy of Kaṃsa, out of compassion,
engaged in water-sports for a moment, and returned again to his father's lap.

Whereupon that best of the Yadus went to the abode of Nanda;
having given the son to Yaśodā, he brought back her daughter.

Then, having reached his own house, the daughter was handed over to his wife.
And the news was received by the enemy of the gods: “Devakī has given birth.”

Messengers set out to bring the son or daughter then.
Arriving, those messengers of Kaṃsa proceeded to take away the daughter.

Violently snatching her away from Devakī and Vasudeva,
she was seized by Kaṃsa's messengers and handed over to the enemy of the gods.

The unassailable great king seized her and became terrified.
[She had] the complexion of pure gold and a face like the full moon;

Kaṃsa, seeing her laughing, with eyes flashing like lightning,
that foremost among demons commanded: “Take her and kill her upon a stone!”

Having received the command, those demons set about to crush her;
[but] with the speed of lightning, Gaurī went into the presence of Śaṅkara.

Gaurī said:
Listen, O king, I shall tell you where your supreme enemy is:
hidden in the abode of Nanda is the one who will slay you, O foremost among demons!

Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that goddess went to her own abode.
Then, hearing the words of the goddess, King Kaṃsa became exceedingly sorrowful.
He said to his sister Pūtanā: “Go to the house of Nanda. / Having slain that son deceitfully, go, [and take] whatever you greatly desire.
I will grant it to you. Go very quickly to kill my enemy, fair one!” / Having received the command, that demoness set out towards Gokula.
Having assumed the form of a beautiful woman by illusion, she entered there into Gokula. / Bearing poison in her breast, she came to kill [him].
She entered unseen at the door of the cowherds' house, / and having gone inside and picked up the infant, she gave him her breast, [and attained] the path of the virtuous.
Then, having overturned the cart, crushed Tṛṇāvarta and others, / and subdued Kālīya, he then went to Madhupurī.
Having gone there, the cruel Kaṃsa was slain, and he conquered Kaṃsa's wrestlers. / This vow of Viṣṇu's birthday has been told to you, O king.
Hearing it, sins are destroyed; what need be said of what will happen to one who performs it? / Any mortal man or any woman who performs this vow of Hari
attains peerless sovereignty, as desired, in another birth. / The third, sixth, and

eighth, eleventh, and fourteenth [lunar days] contaminated by the preceding tithi must never be performed by those desiring dharma, pleasure, and wealth. / Having carefully avoided the eighth combined with the seventh,
the eighth combined with the ninth should be observed even without the asterism [Rohiṇī]. / If the eighth lasts a little at sunrise and the ninth lasts the whole day,
and is joined with Rohiṇī for a muhūrta, the eighth becomes complete. / If the eighth day is accompanied by Rohiṇī on a Wednesday,
or indeed on a Monday, O king, what is the use of ten million other vows performed? / If on the ninth, lasting a little from sunrise, on a Monday or a Wednesday,
even in a hundred years it may or may not be obtained. / The eighth combined with the ninth should not be performed without the asterism.
The eighth joined with Rohiṇī should be performed even if contaminated by the seventh. / When the dark eighth lunar day lasts even for a kalā, a kāṣṭhā, or a muhūrta,
it alone is to be accepted on the ninth, not the one joined with the seventh; / how much more so on a Wednesday, and especially on a Monday?
How much more so when joined with the ninth, granting liberation to ten million ancestors! / One should abandon the eighth contaminated even by a pala of the seventh, O king of kings,

just as a pot of Gaṅgā water touched by a drop of liquor.
Dilīpa said: / By whom was this performed first, and by whom was it revealed? / What is the merit, what is the fruit, O god? Speak, O great sage!
Vasiṣṭha said: / There was a great king named Citrasena, deeply devoted to great sin, / who committed incest and stole the gold of a twice-born.
He was always sated with wine and always indulged in meat not offered in sacrifice; / thus endowed with sin, he was constantly bent on slaughtering living beings.
He always conversed with outcasts and fallen men. / Such as he was, the king set his mind on hunting.
Having spotted a leopard in the forest and surrounded it on all sides, / he spoke this word with alert attention to all the soldiers:
“I alone shall strike it down. Whoever else strikes it, / he shall be put to death, there is no doubt.” The tiger fled along the king’s path.
Though embarrassed, the king then pursued the tiger; / with great trouble and distress, he was resolved to kill the tiger.
Overcome by the distress of hunger and thirst, at dusk on the bank of the Yamunā— / it was the eighth joined with Rohiṇī, the day of the Lord's birth—
the maidens were performing the vow at the Yamunā for the next day, O lord of men, / with various offerings, articles, and very splendid incenses and lamps,
fragrances, flowers, and substances, charming saffron and the like. / Seeing food of many qualities, his mind was eager to eat.
The king said: “For lack of food, my life-breaths will surely depart today!” / The women said: “On Hari's Janmāṣṭamī, food must not be eaten by you, O sinless one.
Whoever eats on Kṛṣṇa's birthday eats vulture's flesh, donkey, crow, / and beef—there is no doubt about this.
What fault has not arisen for men dwelling in this worldly existence, / if Jayantī was not performed by him while life remained in his body, O king?
For him who does not fast on that day, punishment awaits in the abode of Yama. / What is offered by him the ancestors never accept according to rule.
All the ancestors are cast down when a meal is taken on Jayantī.” / Hearing this, the king then observed the vow, O lord of men.

Having brought some flowers, some perfume, and cloth, delighted, / he performed this vow, and broke the fast at the end of the lunar day and asterism. / By the power of this vow, Citrasena [went] to Hari's abode.
Having mounted a celestial chariot, he went together with his ancestors. / The fruit that is attained by going to Mathurā and beholding Kṛṣṇa’s lotus-face,

that fruit is attained by a person from the Kṛṣṇajanmāṣṭamī vow. / The fruit that is attained by going to Dvārakā and seeing Hari, the Lord of the Universe, / that fruit is attained by the wretched by performing the Janmāṣṭamī vow.

4.14.m: Śaunaka said: / Speak, O exceptionally wise one, O ocean of mercy, out of compassion to me, / of the greatness of the brāhmaṇa, the highest among all the castes.
Sūta said: / The brāhmaṇa is indeed the guru of all castes, O best of the twice-born; / he should be known as the refuge of all the gods, the lord Nārāyaṇa in visible form.
Whoever makes a prostration to a brāhmaṇa, an earthly god, with the thought that he is Hari, / his prosperity and the like increase through devotion, O best of the twice-born.
If someone, puffed up with pride, does not bow to a brāhmaṇa upon seeing him, even out of negligence, / Hari ever desires to cut off his head.
Those of sinful minds who hate a brāhmaṇa even when he has committed an offense / are to be known as haters of Hari; they go to a dreadful hell.
If someone looks with anger upon a brāhmaṇa who has approached to make a request, / Death indeed drives a heated needle into both his eyes.
The foolish man, lowest among men, who reviles an earthly god— / the messengers of Yama place heated iron into his mouth.
In whose house an earthly god rich in austerity takes food, / in their house Kṛṣṇa himself takes food along with the gods.
All sins, such as the killing of a twice-born, are destroyed / for that person who honors even a single drop of water from the foot of a brāhmaṇa.
That person who washes the two feet of a twice-born with his hand with devotion— / I tell you the truth—he is liberated from all sins.
A woman who is sonless, or a woman whose children are dead, / becomes one with living sons and daughters by serving the lotus-feet of a twice-born.

Whatever sacred fords exist in the universe, those sacred fords exist in the ocean; / whatever sacred fords exist in the ocean abide in the feet of a twice-born. / He whose head is constantly sprinkled with water from the foot of a twice-born

has bathed in all the sacred fords and is liberated from all sins. / Listen, O Śaunaka, and I will relate the sin-destroying greatness, / an ancient tale of the water from a brāhmaṇa's foot, O rich in asceticism.
Formerly, O best of the twice-born, there was one devoted to the livelihood of a vaiśya,
a śūdra named Bhīma in the Dvāpara age, who had committed a thousand killings of brāhmaṇas. / Cruel and ever self-satisfied, that great [sinner], furthermore with a vaiśya woman,
deviated from the conduct of a śūdra, this Bhīma was a violator of his guru's bed. / Why should I speak of each one? There is no counting of that bandit's
sins, O tiger among sages, of Bhīma of wicked mind. / Once, he went to the house of a brāhmaṇa.
Having gone there, he set his mind upon taking the goods from his house. / There he stayed outside, near the brāhmaṇa's door.
He spoke words full of wretchedness to that god on earth rich in asceticism: / 'O master, hear my plea!' He was thought of as compassionate.
'I am tormented by hunger; give me food, [or] my breath of life will swiftly depart.'
The brāhmaṇa said: / 'O hungry one, hear my word: there is no one here to do / the cooking for me. Take these rice grains and eat at your pleasure.
I have no father, no mother, no son, no brother, / no wife, and no maternal kinsman; they have all died, leaving me behind.
I stay alone in the house, idle, unfortunate; Hari is the guest. / He alone truly exists; I know nothing without Him.'
Bhīma said: / 'I have no one, O best of the twice-born; moreover, I am a Śūdra by caste. / Having performed your service, I will always remain in your dwelling.'
Sūta said: / Having heard his word, that god on earth, delighted then, / having prepared the cooking, swiftly gave him food, O ascetic.
Filled with joy, he too remained there in the twice-born's abode, / performing charming, affectionate service to the god on earth.
[Bhīma thought:] 'Today or tomorrow I will seize his wealth, and mine as well; / when I resolve to take it, I will take it—there is no doubt of this.'
Having reflected thus within his heart, he would speak while doing his duties; / he whose sins were gone took upon his head [the water] used for washing the feet and other rites.
Every day the twice-born sipped water and held the foot-washing water under a pretext. / Once, a thief came to carry off the wealth.
Having unbolted the door at night, he went into the interior of that house. / Seeing Bhīma, he came with a staff in hand to strike him.
The thief, having cut off his head, quickly fled. / Then the soldiers of Viṣṇu, bearing conch, discus, and mace,
arrived to take that Bhīma who had been freed from sin; / and a divine chariot arrived, accompanied by royal swans, O twice-born.

Mounted upon it, he went to the dwelling of Viṣṇu, which is indeed hard to attain. / This glorification of the earthly god has thus been proclaimed by me; / the man who hears it with devotion—his sin is destroyed.

4.15.m: Śaunaka said: / Tell of the glorification that destroys sins, O highly fortunate one. / What is the fruit of Ekādaśī, or what sin would belong to one who does not observe it?
Sūta said: / What glorification of Ekādaśī can I speak of now? / Having heard the name of Ekādaśī, even the messengers of Yama are filled with fear,
and are terrified among all living beings—of this there is no doubt. / Among all vows, the auspicious Ekādaśī is supreme.
Having fasted, one should keep vigil for Viṣṇu and create a grand decoration. / Indeed, that mortal who worships Hari with tulasī leaves,
obtains the fruit of ten million sacrifices by a single leaf, O twice-born. / Whatever sin is declared for having sex with a forbidden woman—
that sin dissolves through fasting on Ekādaśī. / The twice-born who gives a lamp filled with ghee on the day of Viṣṇu,
in the end goes to the city of Viṣṇu, having destroyed darkness by his own radiance. / Blessed indeed are those provinces, and blessed is that king,
in whose kingdom there is a great festival on Hari's day, on Ekādaśī. / During the sleeping of Nārāyaṇa, during His turning upon His side,
and especially on the Awakening [Ekādaśī], those who remain without food— / 'Do not bring into my presence those living beings who have a share in merit!'
—Thus day and night the lord of the ancestors commands his messengers. / Ekādaśī is beloved of the Lord of the World and increases merit.
Viṣṇu indeed burns the body [of one who engages] in eating food upon that day. / Fie upon their life, their wealth! Fie upon their beauty and their conduct,
the most sinful ones who eat food on Ekādaśī, for they are eaters of feces. / On Ekādaśī, O best of the twice-born, having resorted merely to food,
many and diverse sins reside. / Just as there is great defilement in intercourse with women on the new-moon day,
so indeed evil arises from eating food on Ekādaśī. / Those beings become diseased, lame, afflicted with cough, belly-diseases, and leprosy
upon eating food on that day; / they become village pigs and fall into poverty,
bound by kings, O best of the twice-born, upon eating food on that day. / Whatever sins exist in the world, they reside in food,
O vipra, on the day of Hari. For those who take water according to injunction, / there is deliverance from all sins and from hell.
There is no deliverance for men who eat on the day of Hari. / As many morsels of food as men eat on the day of Hari,
for every morsel there arises the sin born of ten million murders of a brāhmaṇa. / Again I speak, again I speak! Let it be heard, let it be heard, O men:
One must not eat, one must not eat, one must not eat on the day of Hari! / Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing in sacred waters such as the Gaṅgā,
or during an eclipse of the moon and sun, by fasting on Ekādaśī / and having worshipped the Lord of Kamalā on it with garlands of blue lotuses,
and having performed the breaking of the fast according to rule, one does not become a receptacle of a mother's womb. / The twice-born who makes decorations in the house of Hari on Ekādaśī,
having attained the supreme goal, shall abide in the abode of Viṣṇu. / Those who, having arrived at Ekādaśī, remain without food,
their residence is perpetually in the city of Viṣṇu—there is no doubt of this. / Those whose mind shines, absorbed in devotion to tulasī,
go to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu—there is no doubt. / Those who have no desire at all for another's wealth,
and who are contented in mind, their place is surely the city of Viṣṇu. / Those best among men who, when a time of famine arrives,
give food to living beings, their place is indeed Hari's abode—of this there is no doubt. / Those mortals who give up their lives to protect cows,
twice-born men, their master, or women, their place is surely the city of Viṣṇu. / Living beings must never observe a fast overlapping with Daśamī;
it is to be shunned, O best of the twice-born, just like proximity to a wicked man. / If Daśamī is conjoined at the time of daybreak,
then Dvādaśī should be fasted on, and the breaking of the fast should be on Trayodaśī. / If the dawn is joined with the residue of Daśamī,
a Vaiṣṇava should not observe the vow of Ekādaśī on that day. / The four ghaṭikās in the morning are called dawn;
this bathing time of ascetics is traditionally held to be equal to Gaṅgā water. / But if Daśamī is observed at the time of dawn,
Ekādaśī must not be performed then, for it destroys dharma, desire, and wealth. / The wise man should abandon an Ekādaśī pierced even slightly by Daśamī,
just as one would abandon a pot of ghee due to contact with a drop of liquor. / Where an Ekādaśī is complete, and it is [present] again on Dvādaśī,
the latter should be observed by ascetics, while the householder should fast on the former. / Where there is a kalā of Ekādaśī, but Dvādaśī is not beyond,
there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices, and the breaking of the fast is on Trayodaśī. / If Ekādaśī is omitted, but the following [day] is joined with Dvādaśī,
the full Dvādaśī should be fasted on, if one desires the supreme goal. / Where an Ekādaśī is complete and is present again at dawn,
the latter must be observed by all, if Dvādaśī lies beyond. / Those men whose minds are absorbed in the vow of Ekādaśī,
Heaven indeed is their abode, and then they go to Hari's dwelling. / There is no means for [attaining] the next world superior to the Ekādaśī.
Even one laden with many sins who observes the day of Hari, / freed from all sins, goes to Hari's abode.
A woman who, along with her husband, observes the day of Hari, / having good sons and blessed with a husband, goes after death to Hari's house.
Whoever out of devotional disposition offers a lamp before Hari / on the day of Hari, O best of the twice-born, the count of his merit is limitless.
The woman who, along with her husband, keeps a vigil for Hari, / shall dwell for a long time in Hari's abode together with her husband, O twice-born.
Whatever article a person gives to Hari with devotion, O twice-born, / on the day of Hari, his merit is indeed imperishable for ever.
Formerly, in the city named Kāñcana, there was a man named Vallabha. / Rich with abundant wealth, he shone like the lord of riches.
His beloved wife was of great beauty, Hemaprabhā by name, O twice-born; / but the overwhelming, harsh quality of Kali afflicted her.
She constantly quarreled with her husband, O man rich in asceticism, / [and] willfully insulted her elders with base speech all the time.
She always ate directly from the cooking pot, secretly and alone, impure, / and gave the leftovers to the elders every day.
Her mind was always fixed on a paramour, yet she proclaimed, "I am a chaste wife!"; / by her quarrels, O brāhmaṇa, she constantly agitated the mind of her husband.
Once, seeing her arrive, her husband rebuked her, / and struck her, who was steeped in every sin, O twice-born.
Filled with rage, she went into a deserted house; / unnoticed, she lay down in a corner and took neither water nor food.
By divine chance, that day was the turning-over [in sleep] of Viṣṇu's side, / the Ekādaśī observance, O brāhmaṇa, which destroys all sins.
Then at dawn, when night [ended], the Dvādaśī combined with Śravaṇa arrived, / and there the woman remained, her mind entirely filled with fury.
Having passed two [days] without food, she indeed became free from impurity; / and in the night of the Jayantī day, she met her death, O twice-born.
Then, by Yama's order, terrifying messengers arrived to take her, / such as she had been, holding nooses and clubs in their hands.
When they bound her and set their minds on taking her to Yama's abode, / just then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived, bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Having cut the noose, they placed her, now purified and freed from sin, / upon a celestial chariot, and conveyed her to the abode of Hari.
Surrounded by them, she went to the auspicious state, difficult even for gods to attain. / Thus the glorification of Viṣṇu's day has been narrated to you, O bull among the twice-born.
Even one who performs it unintentionally goes to Hari's abode. / On the day of Ekādaśī, a mortal who offers a lamp in Hari's house,

even with every step he takes, gains more than the fruit of a horse sacrifice. / Those who listen to and recite the Purāṇas on the day of Hari / obtain with every syllable the fruit born of the gift of a brown cow.

4.16.m: Śaunaka said: / By what action, O Sūta, does the destruction of sins take place, / and may the grace of glorious Hari arise? Tell that out of compassion.
Sūta said: / Listen, O Śaunaka; I shall describe what destroys sins for those who listen, / by which the grace of Viṣṇu arises, effecting the destruction of wicked deeds.
On the full-moon day, O brāhmaṇa, whoever, endowed with devotional disposition, / performs the worship of the glorious Lord of the Universe with various rites,
his defilement accumulated over ten million births is destroyed, O sage; / the grace of this consort of Śrī surely arises upon him.
Whoever gives food with devotion to a twice-born on the Dvādaśī, / his sins perish just as darkness does at the rise of dawn.
The man who bathes glorious Hari with milk, O twice-born, / or with sugar and the like on the Dvādaśī, the favor of glorious Hari is immediately his.
Indeed, whoever offers a flower to glorious Hari without a mantra, O brāhmaṇa, / it is like a stone, and the giver goes to a low destination.
And whatever gift a man gives to an ignorant brāhmaṇa, like a stone, / of that gift there is indeed no merit.
If a twice-born lacking learning accepts a gift out of delusion, foolish in intellect, / it is as if the fire of time were digested; thereby he goes to hell.
Just as a wooden elephant, or just as an antelope in a painting, / so is a twice-born devoid of learning, O brāhmaṇa: these three are holders of names only.
Just as water standing on a road is purified by wind and the sun, / so upon seeing an attendant [of Hari] with devotion, one's sin is destroyed.
The man who, in the month of Āśvina on the full-moon day, / gives parched grain mixed with ghee to glorious Hari, and cowries for play,
through devotion goes to Hari's abode, free from return [to rebirth]; / but the man who out of delusion does not give, to him Hari brings no satisfaction.
For as many cowries as one gives to Hari on the full-moon day / in Āśvina, for that many days he shall certainly dwell in Hari's abode.
Formerly, in the city of Karavīra, there was a merciless śūdra, / named Kāladvija, O best of the twice-born, a terrifying sinner.
Engaged only in his own purpose, he was a ruiner of his master's work. / Once, he died, and the terrifying messengers of Yama
arrived to take him away to the dwelling of Yama. / Having bound him, they brought him, and seeing him, Yama questioned his minister.
Yama said: / O minister, what deeds, auspicious or inauspicious, exist for him? / Tell it completely from its root, O discerning Chitragupta.
Chitragupta said: / This wicked, evil-minded man was a destroyer of his master's work. / There is not an atom's measure of merit; let him be boiled in hell,
and for a hundred manvantaras, O king, let this cruel man dwell in the womb of a serpent, / and taking birth in a stone, dwell perpetually in [someone's] house.
Sūta said: / For that duration of time, O brāhmaṇa, he then fell into hell; / and after that, he was born in a stone cavity into the serpent womb, deeply miserable.
Once, in the month of Āśvina on the full-moon day, O twice-born, / the serpent threw parched grain and a cowrie out from his hole.
It fell before Hari. Hari himself, / the merciful destroyer of grief, swiftly destroyed his sin.
In time, when his time came, he met with his death. / The messengers of Yama arrived in great numbers to fetch him, O twice-born.
When they bound him to lead him to Yama's abode, / just then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived, bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Severing the noose, they placed him, whose sins were now gone, swiftly onto a divine chariot / there, and the messengers of Yama fled.
Surrounded by them, the serpent went to the dwelling of Viṣṇu; / there he stood before Hari, free from returning [to rebirth].
Whoever offers parched grain with ghee and a cowrie to Hari with devotion, O twice-born, / I do not know how immense his merit surely becomes!
Whoever hears this sin-destroying chapter, O brāhmaṇa, / his sins are destroyed by the grace of glorious Hari.

4.17.m: Śaunaka said: / Please also narrate to me from its root the sin-destroying glorification / of Viṣṇu's foot-water, O very wise one, O ocean of mercy.

Sūta said:
Water from Viṣṇu's feet is auspicious, destroying all sins. / Whoever bears even a single drop gains the fruit of all sacred fords.
Water from Viṣṇu's feet, O Brahmin, destroys sin upon mere touch; / there is no untimely death [for him], and he gains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
If a sinner drinks water from Viṣṇu's feet, / the sin lodged in his body is destroyed, O Brahmin; there is no doubt.
The water from Viṣṇu's feet combined with a tulasī leaf, O twice-born, / whoever carries [it] on his head with devotion goes to Hari's abode at the end.
Whatever fruit is obtained by giving gold equal [in weight] to Mount Meru, / that fruit is obtained by men by touching the water from Hari's feet.
Whatever fruit men obtain by giving tens of millions and thousands of cows, / that fruit is certainly obtained by touching the water from [his] feet.
Whatever fruit is obtained by performing tens of millions and thousands of sacrifices, / men [obtain] ten million times that by touching the water from Hari's feet.
Whatever fruit is obtained by people by giving away ten million maidens [in marriage], / by touching water from Viṣṇu's feet, O twice-born, the fruit is greater than that.
By giving ten million elephants, by giving ten million horses, / whatever fruit a mortal obtains [from that, he obtains] by touching the water from Hari's feet.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains by giving the seven continents together with their crops, / by touching the water from Viṣṇu's feet, O Brahmin, he obtains more than that.
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall tell [you] briefly; what more [need be said]? / Touching the water from Viṣṇu's feet, even a sinner goes to Hari's abode.

Śaunaka said:
By touching and drinking [it] in ancient times, what living being reached the abode of Hari? / Tell me [this], O Sūta, out of your compassion.

Sūta said:
In ancient times, in the Tretā age, there was a sinful Brahmin named Sudarśana. / He would constantly eat on the day of Janārdana, O best of the twice-born.
He constantly reviled the scriptures; he always reviled vows. / He knew nothing else apart from his own belly.
Once, when his time had come, he met his death, O twice-born. / The messengers of Yama arrived, bound him, and led him to Yama's abode.
Seeing him, the brother of Yamunā angrily asked his minister: / 'O minister, declare thoroughly his merit and his sin.
This Brahmin is a great sinner; he appears to be one of cruel deeds.'

Citragupta said:
'Listen to his sin; he does not have even an atom of merit. / Even on the day of Hari, he constantly ate food, O lord.
Whatever vile man eats on the day of Kamalā's husband, / he shall eat feces, O king, and go to a dreadful hell.
Assign this one a place in hell for a hundred Manvantaras; / then indeed his birth shall be in the womb of a village pig.'

Sūta said:
Then, by Yama's command, O Brahmin, by his terrifying messengers / he was cast into feces for more than a hundred Manvantaras.
Then he was released and became a village pig on earth. / One must suffer hell for a long time on account of eating on Hari's day.
Then, O Brahmin, his time having come, he passed away; / he obtained rebirth in the womb of a crow, constantly eating feces.
One day, O Brahmin, having drunk water from the feet of glorious Hari / that was standing at a doorway, he was freed from all sins.
On that very day, the crow fell [victim] to a Śabara; / the crow reached the state of death at the proper time by the hunter.
When a divine, auspicious chariot joined with royal swans arrived, / the bird mounted it and went to Hari's temple, O Brahmin.
The glorification of the water from [his] feet, which destroys sins, has been told. / Whatever sinful man hears it, his sin is destroyed.

4.18.m:
Śaunaka said:
If someone, deluded, should approach a forbidden woman, O Sūta, / by what means does his purification come about? Tell [me this] thoroughly.

Sūta said:
If a Brahmin approaches an outcaste woman such as a Caṇḍālī or a Śvapākī, / he should fast for three [days] and then perform the Prājāpatya vow.
He should shave [his head] including the topknot and give two cows; / having given an appropriate priestly fee, that twice-born attains purification.
If a kṣatriya or a vaiśya goes to a Caṇḍāla woman or the like, / he should perform the Prājāpatya penance and give two pairs of cattle.
If a Śūdra pursues a Śvapākī woman, O rich in asceticism, / he should give four pairs of cattle and perform the Prājāpatya vow.
If, deluded, he approaches his mother, sister, own daughter, / or daughter-in-law, he should then perform three Kṛcchra penances.
Having performed three Cāndrāyaṇa penances, he should give three pairs of cattle; / having shaved [his head] including the topknot, he should then drink pañcagavya.
And when an offering is made into the fire here, in this way he is purified, O rich in asceticism. / [If he approaches] the father's wife, O best of the twice-born, or his mother's sister,
the guru's wife, a maternal uncle's wife, a brother's wife, or a woman of his own gotra, / if he approaches [any of them] out of delusion, he should perform two Prājāpatyas,
three Cāndrāyaṇas, O Brahmin, and give five pairs of cattle / as a priestly fee to Brahmins; he is purified, there is no doubt here.
The fool who approaches a cow should fast for three [days]; / having given a cow and also food, he is purified here, there is no doubt.
[If he approaches] a prostitute, a female donkey, a sow, a female monkey, or a female buffalo, O twice-born, / having immersed himself up to the neck in mud of cow dung and water,
he should remain there without food; he is purified in just three nights. / Having shaved [his head] including the topknot, he should fast for three nights;
staying in water for one night, he is certainly purified, there is no doubt. / But when a man, deluded by passion, approaches a Brahmin woman,
he should perform three Prājāpatyas and three Cāndrāyaṇas; / he should also give three cows; he is certainly purified, O rich in asceticism.
The Brahmin woman should drink pañcagavya for five nights, O twice-born, / and give two cows as a priestly fee; she is purified here, there is no doubt.
When one goes to another's woman, he should perform the Sāṃtapana penance. / As is a crossbar, so is a woman; therefore, one should avoid her.
If a man should go even once to an outcaste, low-born woman, / he should perform the Prājāpatya penance; he is surely purified, there is no doubt.
A woman is like a burning coal; a man is like a pot of clarified butter. / One should never stay in her vicinity, O Brahmin.
A woman who conceives a child by a paramour, bringing ruin to her family, / must be abandoned in every way, O Brahmin; there is no fault in that.
A woman who leaves home, abandoning even her own kin, / is ruined and cast out of the family; there is to be no association with her again.
When a woman goes, bewildered, to another man, / she should perform the Prājāpatya penance and then drink pañcagavya.
She should then give two cows; she is certainly purified, there is no doubt. / If a foolish Brahmin woman, O Brahmin, deluded, goes to another man,

she should then be abandoned by people; there is no fault [in that]. / If an earthly god Brahmin, deluded by lust, approaches a Brahmin woman, / he should then give a cow and sesame seeds; he is purified here, there is no doubt.

4.19.m: Śaunaka said: / Having consumed feces and urine out of ignorance, or having touched liquor, / I shall explain how their purification takes place; listen, O twice-born.
One should perform two Prājāpatya vows, visit sacred bathing places, O sage, / give a gift of a bull and eleven cows, and then shave [one's head] along with the topknot.
Having gone to a crossroads, [performing] the entire Prājāpatya vow likewise, / one should then give two cows, and then drink the five products of the cow.
Having fed the brāhmaṇas, he is indeed purified; there is no doubt about this. / If, even knowingly in times of distress, any man eats the food
If a man eats [such forbidden food], he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; / having shaved his head including the lock of hair, he should then drink pañcagavya.
One, two, three, or four cows should be given to brāhmaṇas respectively. / If one consumes the food of a śūdra, food during birth-pollution, uneatable food, or water,
or the leftovers of a śūdra, knowingly or in times of distress, / he should perform two Prājāpatyas and likewise three Cāndrāyaṇas.
He should then give two cows, and drink the five products of the cow, O twice-born. / Having offered oblations into the fire and fed many brāhmaṇas, he certainly becomes pure.
If food has been eaten by mice, mongooses, or cats, O twice-born, / sprinkling it with water mixed with sesame seeds and darbha grass purifies it; there is no doubt.
If any man eats onion, garlic, horseradish, bottle-gourd, carrots, or meat, / O brāhmaṇa, he should observe the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
A śūdra fond of liquor and meat, through following vile deeds— / a brāhmaṇa should avoid such a śūdra from afar, as if he were an outcaste.
Those who are devoted to serving twice-borns, free from liquor and meat, / and dedicated to giving gifts and their own duties, are to be known as the best of śūdras.
If brāhmaṇas eat out of ignorance during [the impurity of] birth or death, / a brāhmaṇa becomes pure through ten thousand [recitations of the] Gāyatrī.
A kṣatriya [becomes pure] with [the same number of] thousands, a vaiśya with five thousand, / and even a śūdra becomes purified through the five products of the cow, O you rich in asceticism.
If one drinks ghee, water, or yogurt placed in a vessel belonging to a low-caste person, / whatever caste he belongs to, even if done out of ignorance, he should perform the Prājāpatya vow.
He should give a generous gift, and is purified by fire according to the rule. / Even for śūdras there is no fasting; one is purified through gifts alone.
One should shave [one's head] along with the topknot after fasting for a day and a night. / A man who is struck with sticks and the like by low-caste men, O twice-born,
should perform the Prājāpatya vow, or else the Cāndrāyaṇa vow; / and having shaved [his head] along with the topknot, he should then drink the five products of the cow.
He should then give two cows, and offer food and other offerings into the fire. / If any man knowingly or unintentionally eats where liquor is drunk in the house, O brāhmaṇa,
that man is also to be cast out from the family. / A brāhmaṇa who destroys the seed of a cow, or cuts off its tail,
One who steals gold should perform three Prājāpatya penances; / having shaved his head including the lock of hair, he should likewise drink pañcagavya.
Having offered oblations into the fire according to the rule, he should likewise give three cows. / Only then may his water and food be accepted, O you rich in asceticism.
One should eat [unsolicited food] in the morning for three days, and unsolicited food in the evening for three days, / and then not eat at all for three days; this is the Prājāpatya vow.

Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, ghee, and water with kuśa grass— / a brāhmaṇa should drink these for two days, fasting for one night; / this Sāṃtapana penance, O sage, is declared to remove all sins.
Eating a single morsel in the morning for three days, and one unsolicited in the evening for three days, / and then fasting for three days; this vow is the Atikṛcchra.
For three days each, O twice-born one, he should drink hot water, milk, and ghee, / bathing once; this Taptakṛcchra, O sage, is declared to remove sins.
Abstaining from food for twelve days is the penance that destroys sin; / it is known by the name Parāka, and is renowned, O you rich in asceticism.

One should increase one mouthful each day during the bright fortnight, and decrease it in the dark fortnight, / not eating on the day the moon disappears; this is traditionally known as the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Collected in mind, a brāhmaṇa should eat four mouthfuls in the morning, / and four when the sun has set; this is known as the Śiśucāndrāyaṇa.

A woman who cuts a pumpkin gourd should drink the five products of the cow for three days; / she should donate five pumpkin gourds along with gold and garments. / Only then may her water and cooked food be accepted, O you rich in asceticism.

4.20.m: Śaunaka said: / What good deed has been declared by doing which people will cross the ocean of worldly existence / in the Kali age, O Sūta, like frogs in a dark well?
Sūta said: / In the month of Kārttika, which is dear to Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, one should take a morning bath, / and, concentrated in mind, worship Rādhā and Dāmodara with devotion.
Giving up deceit and the like, O brāhmaṇa, and devoted to the service of her husband, / she goes to glorious Hari's abode, known as Goloka, which is very difficult to attain.
She who offers incense and a lamp to Rādhā and Dāmodara in Kārttika / goes to Viṣṇu's abode, freed from her sins.

The woman who gives garments at the abode of Rādhā and Dāmodara in Kārttika, O brāhmaṇa, / dwells with glorious Hari for a long time.

She who offers fragrant flowers and a garland to Rādhā and Dāmodara / in the month of Kārttika goes to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
She who also gives perfume, food offerings, sugar, and other things / to Rādhā and Dāmodara goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whatever she gives to a twice-born in Kārttika, O brāhmaṇa, / for the pleasure of Rādhā and Dāmodara, her merit becomes imperishable.
The woman who worships Rādhā and Dāmodara with devotion in the morning / during Kārttika, O twice-born, does not go to hell for a long time.
Never on this earth will she become a widow in birth after birth, / nor will she ever become unpleasant to her husband, as occurred before.
Formerly, in the Tretā age, O brāhmaṇa, there was a śūdra named Śaṅkara, / who lived in the Saurāṣṭra region; his wife was named Kalipriyā.
She constantly longed for a paramour, and regarded her husband as mere straw, thinking: / 'This husband is not fit for me; another man is my master.'
Thinking thus, she constantly gives him the leftovers [of food]; / through association with the vile, the greatly deluded woman ate meat and drank liquor.
Cruel as she was, she continually insulted her husband at will, [thinking:] / 'He is a shackle on my feet; why hasn't he died yet?
When he is dead, I will enjoy pleasures as I please.' / Reasoning thus in her heart, that foolish woman then, with a paramour,
made a pact: 'We two shall go to another country,' O twice-born. / At night, while her husband was asleep, [she cut] his throat with a sword, O twice-born.
Having cut [his throat] for the sake of the paramour, she went to the rendezvous spot. / The paramour who had arrived had been devoured by a leopard, O twice-born.
Seeing this, she wept and fell down in a faint. / Having recovered after a long time, the foolish woman lamented piteously:
By fate, a tiger has devoured that lover who was my master. / What shall I do? Where shall I go? I have been deceived by the creator!'
Sūta said: / Then, O brāhmaṇa, Kalipriyā returned to her own house; / placing her face on her husband's mouth, she wept aloud:
Kalipriyā said: / 'Alas, my lord, what an exceedingly dreadful deed have I done! / To what realm shall I go? Speak a few words, O husband!'
"Reproach me as much as you wish, for I am thoroughly blamed. / You say nothing, my lord; there is no other refuge for me."
Sūta said: / She bowed at his feet and went to another city. / Entering there, the woman saw many virtuous people,
Devoted to the morning bath in the month of Ūrja and Vaiṣṇavas in the Narmadā, / And women also at the river, O twice-born, [worshiping] Rādhā and Dāmodara,
And worship being performed with sounds of conches and great festivities, / With fragrances, flowers, incenses, lamps, garments, and various fruits,
And with mouth-perfumes. Endowed with devotion and filled with humility upon seeing [it], / She asked: "Tell me, women, what is this being done?"
The women said: / "In Ūrja, the best of all months, [we worship] the auspicious Rādhā and Dāmodara. / Having performed this worship, O mother, which removes all sins and brings auspiciousness,
Sin accumulated over ten million births is destroyed, and an abode is attained." / Renouncing meat, she performed worship on the day of Hari;
She met her death on the full moon day, purified, O twice-born. / The servants of Yama quickly arrived at his abode
To take her, filled with wrath, and bound her with leather ropes. / Then the messengers of Viṣṇu arrived in a chariot made of gold,
Bearing conch, discus, mace, and lotus, wearing forest garlands. / They struck with the edges of their discuses, and the messengers of Yama fled.
Mounted on the golden aerial chariot yoked with royal swans, O twice-born, / Surrounded by them, she went to the abode of Viṣṇu.
There she dwelt for a long time, enjoying pleasures as she desired. / The woman who worships Rādhā and Dāmodara in Kārttika, O twice-born,

Goes, with sins abandoned through worship, to the charming place named Goloka. / Whatever man or woman hears this with devotion and concentrated mind, / The sin accumulated over ten million births of his or hers is destroyed.

4.21.m: Śaunaka said: / "Speak, O sage Sūta, of the rule for Kārtika, the best of all months; / You ought to explain the observances fully."
Sūta said: / "On the full moon day of Āśvina, O best of the twice-born, one should maintain focus / And perform the vow of Kārtika until the Awakening [Eleventh]."
By day, O twice-born, a man should discharge urine and feces facing north; / Let him be silent and fully mindful, and at night facing south.
On the path, in water, in cowpens, in cremation grounds, or on an anthill, O twice-born, / One observing the vow should never discharge urine or feces.
One should not discharge feces or urine in very excellent places. / Having taken clean clay, one should then wash the left hand.
For purification with water and clay, the count was formerly twenty: / one on the penis, five on the anus, and ten on the left hand.
Ten times on both hands, and three times each on the feet. / Then he should cleanse his mouth and make the resolve for the bath.
Meditating on Dāmodara in the heart, he should then recite this mantra: / 'In Kārtika, I shall perform the morning bath, O Janārdana,
For the pleasure of Dāmodara along with Rādhā, destroying sins. / Salutation to the lotus-navelled one, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who reclines on the waters;
Salutations to You along with Rādhā! Accept the argha-offering; be gracious to me!' / Then he should bathe, O twice-born, and apply the forehead mark according to rule.
If one performs any rite devoid of the upright mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), / All that work is fruitless; this truth is spoken by me.
The body of men made without an upright mark / Should not be looked upon; having seen it, one should gaze upon the sun.
On whose forehead a white upright mark made with clay is seen, / Even an outcaste is a purified soul and worthy of worship, without doubt. / But those vile men who make an upright mark without a gap,
On their foreheads is always the footprint of a dog, without doubt. / Having completed the duty prescribed for the morning, [the plant] beloved of Hari,
Namely tulasī, which destroys sins, he should worship with devotion, O twice-born. / Then, hearing the Purāṇic narrative of glorious Hari with a steady mind,
The observer of the vow should worship a twice-born man with devotion according to rule. / Another's seat, another's food, another's bed, another's wife:
One should always avoid these, O twice-born, and especially in Kārttika. / Sour gruel, black gram, meat, and honey,
Kidney beans and the like, the observer of the vow should continually avoid in Kārtika; / Lime, meat, lime-powder, and stale food, O twice-born.
Lentil is proclaimed among grains, [yet] milk of cows is not meat. / Salt produced from the earth, O twice-born, and parts of living beings are indeed meat;
All liquids purchased from a twice-born, and water situated in a small pond. / Celibacy, dining in the fourth part of the day from a leaf-plate,
A tiger among the twice-born should observe, and avoid anointing with oil; / Mushrooms, radish stalks, asafoetida, onion, pūtikā leaves,
Garlic, radish, horseradish, and likewise bottle gourd fruit, / Wood-apple, eggplant, ash gourd, and eating from bell-metal,
Twice-cooked food, food from a woman in childbirth, fish, a bed, a menstruating woman, / Eating twice or thrice, and contact with women, the observer of the Kārtika vow should avoid.
The householder should always abandon myrobalan on a Sunday, O twice-born. / Through ash gourd, there is loss of wealth; through bṛhatī, one forgets Hari;
Through pointed gourd, there is no prosperity; through radish, loss of strength; / One becomes stained through bilva fruit, and is born in animal wombs through lime;
Through palm fruit, there is destruction of the body; through coconut, foolishness; / Bottle gourd is equal to beef; there is cow-slaughter through watermelon;
Flat bean is said to cause sin; pūtikā is like killing a brahmin; / Through eggplant, loss of sons occurs; through black gram, one becomes chronically ill;
Through meat, great sin arises; he should avoid these on the first day and subsequent days [of the fortnight]. / Whatever food one avoids for the pleasure of glorious Hari, O twice-born,
That, again, after giving it to a brahmin at the end of the vow, becomes his food. / Regarding the man observing the Kārtika vow and acting according to instruction, O twice-born,
The messengers of Yama flee, just as elephants seeing a lion. / The vow of Viṣṇu is supreme, O twice-born; a hundred sacrifices are not equal to it.
Having performed a sacrifice, one goes to heaven; the observer of the Kārtika vow goes to Vaikuṇṭha. / Whatever evil deed has arisen from the actions of mind, speech, and body, O twice-born,
Dissolves in an instant upon seeing the observer of the Kārtika vow. / Even the four-faced Brahmā is not capable of describing
The merit of the observer of the Kārttika vow who performs it as prescribed. / Upon doing this, all sins flee in the ten directions, O twice-born, [saying]:
'Where shall I go? Where shall I dwell out of fear of the observer of the Kārttika vow?' / On the full moon day, according to one's capacity, food, clothing, and the like, O twice-born,

He should give for the pleasure of glorious Hari, and feed the brahmins as well. / At night, the observer of the vow should keep vigil with dances, songs, and the like. / Whoever hears this with devotion, his sin is destroyed.

4.22.m: Śaunaka said: / "Speak, O omniscient one, of the glorification that destroys sins for those who listen, / For the benefit of all living beings, out of compassion, concerning tulasī."
Sūta said: / O twice-born, in whose surroundings stands a grove of Tulasī, / because his house has the nature of a sacred site, Yama's servants do not come.
O brāhmaṇa, the grove of Tulasī is auspicious and removes all sins; / the best of men plant it, and thereby they do not see the son of the Sun.
Whoever should plant, protect, attend, see, or touch it, / all his sin would be destroyed, O best of the twice-born.
