Those who worship Hari with tender leaves of Tulasī, / those high-minded men, O brāhmaṇa, do not go to the abode of Death.
The best rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Maheśvara, / along with the gods and sacred sites beginning with Puṣkara, abide in a Tulasī leaf.
A sinner who, in contact with leaves of Tulasī, gives up his vital breaths, / goes to the abode of Viṣṇu: this has been spoken by me in truth.
A man smeared with the clay of Tulasī, even if bound by hundreds of sins, / when he yields up his vital breaths, goes to the temple of Hari.
The man who bears Tulasī-wood and sandalwood, O brāhmaṇa, / sin does not touch his body; he goes to the supreme state.
He who wears a garland of Tulasī-wood around his neck, / even if impure or ill-behaved, goes through devotion to the home of Hari.
On whose body is seen a garland made of dhātrī fruits / or arising from Tulasī-wood, he indeed is a Bhāgavata man.
He who wears around his neck a garland made of Tulasī leaves / that is the remainder from Viṣṇu's offering, is especially worthy of reverence by the gods.
Furthermore, he who, having placed a Tulasī garland on his neck, / worships Janārdana, obtains with each flower the merit of ten thousand cows.
Those rationalists of sinful minds who do not wear the garland, / burned by the fire of Hari's anger, do not return from hell.
One should not abandon the garland of Tulasī, especially the garland of dhātrī, / which destroys mortal sins and grants duty, desire, and wealth.
As many body hairs of men as the garland of dhātrī touches in the Kali [age], / for that many thousands of years does he reside in Keśava's abode.
Offering the garland made of Tulasī-wood to Keśava, / the man who wears it with devotion has no sin at all.
Seeing a garland of Tulasī-wood, the messengers of the King of Ghosts / flee far away, like a leaf tossed by the wind.
In a forest of Tulasī, in the shade of a dhātrī, the best of men / who offers an ancestral ball of rice—his ancestors attain liberation, O best of the twice-born.
He who holds a dhātrī fruit in his hand, on his head, on his neck, / at his ears, and in his mouth, O twice-born, is to be known as Hari himself.
If a twice-born brāhmaṇa worships Śrī Hari with dhātrī leaves and fruits, / sin accumulated through ten million births is destroyed by that single worship.
Sacrifices, gods, sages, and sacred sites in Kārttika, O twice-born, / taking refuge in the dhātrī tree, always abide [there] in Kārttika.
The man who plucks a dhātrī leaf in Kārttika, or a Tulasī leaf on the twelfth lunar day, / would go to hell, full of torment.
O brāhmaṇa, he who eats food in the shade of a dhātrī in Kārttika, / his sin arising from the contact of food is destroyed for a year.
In the midst of a Tulasī grove and at the foot of a dhātrī in Kārttika, / whoever performs worship of Hari, O brāhmaṇa, surely goes to Vaikuṇṭha.
The water staying at the base of a Tulasī, O best of the twice-born, / which a sinner receives upon his head with devotion, goes to the house of Hari.
He who carries on his head water dripping from a Tulasī leaf, / has bathed in all sacred sites, and in the end goes to the house of Hari.
Long ago in the Dvāpara age, O great sage, there was a certain best of the twice-born; / having bathed one day, and given an oblation of water to Tulasī, he went home.
He was Āditya by name, radiant like the sun by his merit. / A certain eater afflicted by thirst, possessing many sins, arrived.
Drinking water from the base of the Tulasī, his sin was destroyed. / Quickly a hunter also arrived, Asimardana by name.
He said: 'Has the food been eaten, and after eating, have you broken [it] and gone away? / Why, having made [a mess] of what was in my cooking pot, have you come, you injurer?'
He struck him dead. To take him away by the command of Yama, / angry servants arrived, noose and club in hand.
They resolved to bind and lead him away, when the servants of Viṣṇu arrived. / Then, cutting the leather noose, upon a charming chariot,
they quickly made him mount. Filled with modesty, they asked: / 'By what merit, O good sirs, is he indeed being carried away?'
They said: 'Long ago this man was a king; he performed very great merit. / [Yet] he abducted a certain beautiful woman.'
'Because of this sin, the king went to the abode of Yama. / There distress was indeed inflicted by you all at Yama's command.'
'He lay down and engaged in sport with a woman made of copper / on a burning iron bed, [experiencing] despair due to his action, O king.'
'A fearful, hot iron pillar was heated by Yama's order; / then, standing embracing it, the king experienced sorrow for a long time.'
'He was sprinkled with streams of caustic water by others in the abode of Yama; / then, at the conclusion of hell, again and again in a womb of sin,'
'having obtained birth, he experienced sorrow for a long time by his own karma. / By drinking water from the base of the Tulasī, he goes to the home of Hari.'
Now, having heard that speech, the messengers went just as they had come. / Along with him, the messengers of Viṣṇu went to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
The sin-destroying glorification of Tulasī has been related, O brāhmaṇa. / What might become of those who render service with devotion, I do not know, O sage!

4.23.m: Śaunaka said: / Speak, O sage Sūta, out of compassion, the glorification / that destroys impurities, of the remaining five days of Kārttika.
Sūta said: / Hear, O Śaunaka, what has been asked, the sin-destroying glorification; / I will tell of the remaining five days of the month of Ūrja.
O tiger among sages, the Viṣṇupañcaka is the foremost of observances; / during it, whoever worships Śrī Hari with Rādhā with devotion,
with fragrant pastes, flowers, incenses, lamps, garments, and various fruits, / freed from all sins, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
A student of the Veda, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic / does not attain the supreme place without performing the Viṣṇupañcaka.
The renowned Viṣṇupañcaka is meritorious and removes all sins; / whoever performs a bath during it obtains the fruit of all sacred sites.
Before Śrī Hari, O brāhmaṇa, and near a Tulasī, / whoever should offer with devotional disposition a lamp filled with clarified butter,
in the sky for the pleasure of Śrī Hari, he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu; / even a sinner goes to the abode of Hari: this has been spoken by me in truth.
And if one bathes Acyuta with devotion, with honey, milk, ghee, and so on, / pleased, what will Hari not give to that good person?
One should offer sweet milk-rice as an offering to the Lord of the lords of gods; / the four-faced [Brahmā] is unable to enumerate his merit.
Having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa on the eleventh lunar day with concentrated mind, / having properly obtained cow dung, one attends [it] with mantras.
The observer of the vow should again consume cow urine with mantras on the twelfth day, / milk on the thirteenth, and curd on the fourteenth.
Having obtained [these] for the purification of sins, fasting for four days, / on the fifth day he should bathe and worship Keśava according to the rule,
feed brāhmaṇas with devotion, and give them a fee; / then at night he should consume properly consecrated five products of the cow.
He who is unable to do so should eat fruits and roots, / or he may consume oblation food, O brāhmaṇa, according to the prescribed rule.
He who observes the five-day vow of Śrī Hari, O brāhmaṇa, and worships him with tulasī leaves, / is to be recognized as the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
Long ago in the Tretā age there was a śūdra dedicated to the occupation of a bandit, / by name Daṇḍakara, who constantly reviled dharma.
He was a speaker of untruth, a killer of friends, lusting after the charms of courtesans, / a robber of brāhmaṇas' property, cruel, and delighting in intercourse with other men's wives.
He killed those who sought refuge, kept company with heretics, / ate beef, drank liquor, and constantly reviled others.
He betrayed trust and destroyed the livelihood of his kinsmen, O best of the twice-born. / Seeing such a wicked man in his house, the twice-born,
"Hey, you fool, evil-doer! Ruin is being brought upon / the reputation that was earned by our ancestors in our spotless lineage!"
Enraged thus, O best of the twice-born, and out of fear of ill repute, / they all abandoned family respect for that foremost among sinners.
Then, having lost all his wealth, he went to the great forest; / he would constantly carry out banditry together with bandits.
Out of fear for those traveling on the road, O brāhmaṇa, they obtained nothing to eat; / tormented by hunger, they went to another place.
Entering there, they all saw many virtuous people, / Vaiṣṇavas, the best among the twice-born, seated at the root of a dhātrī tree, O brāhmaṇa.
All those bandits went away, O brāhmaṇa, but that Daṇḍakara / approached their presence and bowed down.
Daṇḍakara said: / "I am afflicted by hunger, O best of the twice-born; my vital breaths will surely depart. / Give me something to eat! I have come to you for refuge."
Hearing his word, those devoted to dharma said to him: / "During the renowned Viṣṇupañcaka, which removes all sins,
how is it that you desire to eat food today, on the day of Hari? / Tell in detail: what is your name now?"
He said joyfully to the brāhmaṇas: "I am known by name as Daṇḍakara. / I am laden with every sin; how can my deliverance come about?"
They said to him: "Perform the best vow, the Viṣṇupañcaka!" / By the command of the brāhmaṇas, O twice-born, he performed the Viṣṇupañcaka.
Having died, he ascended a splendid chariot and went to Hari's abode; / attaining the form of Śrī Hari, he remained free from rebirth.
Whoever hears this sin-destroying narrative with devotion, / their sin accumulated over ten million births is destroyed in that very instant.

4.24.m: Śaunaka said: / "O best among the wise, knower of truth, tell me now, O great-minded sage, / in order, the glorification of gifts."
Sūta said: / "The gift of land, O best of sages, is considered the foremost among gifts. / By him who has made that gift, the fruit of all gifts is deemed to be obtained.
He who gives land bearing crops to a brāhmaṇa, O best of the twice-born, / enjoys happiness in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as fourteen Indras reign.
Then, attaining birth on earth as a sovereign king, / having enjoyed the entire earth for a long time, he goes to the abode of Śrī Hari.
He who gives to a twice-born a plot of land measuring a cowhide / goes to Hari's abode, freed from all sins.
Where a hundred cows and one bull can stand without restraint, / the great sages declare that land to be measured as a cowhide.
Both the leader of land and the giver of land go to heaven; / land should be accepted by wise twice-born persons, even setting aside hundreds of other gifts.
An ignorant brāhmaṇa who, deluded, rejects land, / that twice-born would become an experiencer of extreme misery in birth after birth.
Having obtained land from another, whoever gives it to a twice-born— / to him the Lord of the World grants the supreme state, O brāhmaṇa.
He who seizes land, whether given by himself or given by another, O twice-born, / goes along with ten million families to a most terrible hell.
Whoever steals land belonging to gods or brāhmaṇas, O brāhmaṇa, / no expiation is seen for him even in hundreds of millions of cosmic ages, O sage.
The king who protects land given by another, O twice-born, / his merit becomes ten million times greater than that of the giver.
The merit that is obtained by giving the earth with its seven continents, O twice-born, / that merit a mortal obtains by giving a milk cow to a twice-born.
He who gives a bull to a poor family man, / being completely freed from all sins, goes to the world of Śiva.
He who gives to a brāhmaṇa gold even of the measure of a sesame seed / goes to Hari's abode along with ten million families.
Whoever gives silver to a virtuous brāhmaṇa, O twice-born, / reaches the world of the Moon and drinks nectar there forever.
He who gives coral, pearls, diamond, and gems, / O best of the twice-born, goes to the heavenly realm.
The merit a person attains by the gift of a man's weight in gold— / by giving a śālagrāma stone he obtains ten million times more than that.
The merit one obtains by giving the earth of seven continents along with its mountains and forests, / indeed, that belongs to the giver of a śālagrāma stone.
He who gives a śālagrāma stone to a brāhmaṇa, / by him, O twice-born, the fourteen worlds are given.
He who makes the gift of a man's weight in gold, O bull among the twice-born, / has no rebirth in a mother's womb.
The man who gives an adorned maiden, O best of the twice-born, / goes to Brahmā's abode; there is no rebirth for him.
For a seller of a maiden there is no release from hell; / for a giver of a maiden there is no return from heaven.
He who gives shoes or a parasol to a twice-born, / having died, goes to the city of Indra and dwells there for four cosmic ages.
He who gives divine garment to a virtuous twice-born, / wearing divine clothing in heaven, dwells there for a long time, O best of the twice-born.
Whoever gives an old cow, worn-out cloth, O twice-born, / or a maiden who has already menstruated, goes likewise to hell.
A wise man should not look at the face of a seller of a maiden, O brāhmaṇa; / and if he has seen it through ignorance, he should gaze upon the sun.
A man who gives fruit goes to heaven, O best of the twice-born, / and enjoys fruit resembling nectar there for thousands of cosmic ages.
The mortal who gives vegetables goes to Śiva's abode, O twice-born, / and enjoys for two cosmic ages rice milk that is hard even for the gods to obtain.
The giver of clarified butter, the giver of curds, the giver of buttermilk, and the giver of milk, / having gone to Viṣṇu's abode, drinks nectar.
A mortal who gives perfume and gives flowers goes to the abode of the gods; / adorned with perfumes and flowers, he remains there for thousands of yugas.
He who gives the gift of a bed—the essence of gifts—to a brāhmaṇa, / goes to the abode of Brahmā and rests on a couch for a long time.
The giver of a seat and the giver of a lamp, freed from all evil deeds, / sits on a throne in heaven surrounded by rows of blazing lamps.
The man who gives betel enjoys the entire earth happily; / asleep in heaven on the lap of a divine woman, he surely chews betel.
The best of men who makes the gift of knowledge, the foremost of gifts, / dwells after death in the presence of Viṣṇu for three hundred cosmic ages.
Attaining knowledge there, rare indeed [to obtain], O best of the twice-born, / he attains rare liberation through the grace of glorious Hari, O twice-born one.
The best of men who teaches a helpless, suffering vipra / goes to the dwelling of glorious Hari, freed from rebirth.
The man who gives a manuscript, endowed with devotion and faith, / obtains for each syllable the merit produced by the gift of ten million brown cows.
A mortal who gives honey and gives jaggery goes to the ocean of sugarcane juice; / and the man who bestows salt goes to the world of Varuṇa.
Among all gifts, food and water, O best of the twice-born, / are proclaimed the best by all the sages who know reality.
By him who has given food and water on the surface of the earth, O best of the twice-born, / all gifts have been given, O bull among the twice-born.
The man who is a giver of food, O vipra, is proclaimed a giver of life; / therefore, the giver of food obtains the fruit of all gifts.
As is food, so is water: both are proclaimed to be equal; / and without water, food cannot be prepared, O best of the twice-born.
Hunger and thirst, O tiger among the twice-born, both are proclaimed to be equal; / therefore both food and water are declared to be foremost by the wise.
The best of men who give food on the earth, O brāhmaṇa, / freed from all sins, go to the abode of Hari.
As many morsels of food, O vipra, as one gives on the circle of the earth, / just so many killings of a brāhmaṇa are destroyed, O ascetic.
The sins of those who give gifts of food suddenly leave their bodies / and go to the limbs of those who receive them, O Śaunaka.
Therefore, the wise do not accept food from the most sinful; / the fools who receive it out of delusion become partakers of sin.
Should one place even a single [vessel of] water on the ground, O best of the twice-born, / he would be freed from all sins and go to the abode of Hari.
With effort, O best of the twice-born, the accumulation of wealth should be made; / and accumulated wealth, O brāhmaṇa, one should apply to the act of giving.
Those who hoard wealth out of miserliness are exceedingly miserable; / in the end, abandoning all wealth, they depart destitute, O sage.
Those men who always give gifts again and again and become poor— / they should not be considered poor; they are great lords in the human world.
In the next world, O tiger among the twice-born, lacking the restraint of the virtuous, / merciless, and destitute of kin, what was not given does not wait upon one.
Though wealth exists, the man who neither eats nor gives / should be recognized as truly poor; having died, he heaves sighs [of despair].
Giving is declared to be better even than austerity by the seers of reality; / therefore, with effort, O best of the twice-born, one should perform the act of giving.
If a giver, having set aside [a gift], does not give it to a twice-born, / he goes to a terrible hell that causes fear to all creatures.
If the giver does not remember the gift, and the recipient does not ask for it, / there is residence in hell for both of them as long as the moon and the sun endure.
Whatever sins there are, such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa, O best of the twice-born, / they are destroyed by giving; therefore, one should practice giving.

4.25.m: Śaunaka said: / The glorious deeds of Viṣṇu destroy all calamities, / effect the destruction of all sins, and ward off malignant planets.
They bestow nearness to Viṣṇu and grant the fruits of the four aims of life; / the man who hears them with devotion goes in the end to the house of Hari.
The glorification of the utterance of the name is heard to be greatly wonderful, / by the mere utterance of which a man would go to the supreme state.
Speak now of that rule regarding the chanting of the name, O Sūta. / Sūta said: / Listen, O Śaunaka; I shall tell of the dialogue that is the means to liberation.
Nārada formerly questioned the Kumāra; I shall tell you that. / Once, seated on the bank of the Yamunā with a tranquil mind,
Nārada, with folded hands, asked Sanatkumāra, / having heard of the various kinds of dharmas and the transgressions of dharma.
Glorious Nārada said: / That transgression of dharma among men which has been spoken of by the Lord— / how can its destruction take place? Let it be told, O beloved of the Lord.
Glorious Sanatkumāra said: / Listen, O Nārada, dear to Govinda, knower of the dharma of Govinda, / to that cause of the liberation of the world beyond darkness which you have asked.
Those devoid of all proper conduct, deceitful in mind, outcasts, deceivers of the world, / devoted to hypocrisy, egotism, drinking, and slander, and those who are cruel and sinful,
and whatever others are devoted [only] to wealth, wife, and son, all of them base— / taking refuge at the lotus feet of glorious Govinda, they surely become pure, O twice-born one.
Yet people who are bent on offenses transgress even that divine, / compassionate, supreme [name] that grants liberation to the immovable and the moving; truly, the Name casts them down here.
Even one who commits all offenses is freed when taking refuge in Hari; / but whoever commits offenses against Hari is a defiler among two-legged beings.
If he should ever take refuge in the Name, he surely crosses over through the Name; / for through offense against the Name, which is the friend of all, one falls down.
Glorious Nārada said: / What are those offenses committed against the Name of the Lord, O chief of vipras, / which destroy men's merit and bring them into ordinary worldly existence?
Whoever here sees all the qualities, names, and the like of auspicious, glorious Viṣṇu / as different in his intellect—he indeed works against the Name of Hari.

Disregard of the guru, censure of the Vedic scriptures, and interpreting the Name of Hari as mere praise or inventing it— / for him whose mind turns to sin through offense against the Name, there is no purification even by the Yamas.

Equating [the Name] with all auspicious rites such as dharma, vows, renunciation, and oblations is negligence; / and instructing one who lacks faith, is averse, or will not listen is an offense against the auspicious Name.

Even after hearing the glorification of the Name, that base person who is devoid of love, / clinging to 'I' and 'mine' and the like, is also an offender against the Name.

Thus, out of compassion, the highest, happiness-bearing name of the Lord / was spoken to me by Śaṃkara, O Nārada, which is always to be recited diligently by sages.
Those who, even though knowing, do not quickly avoid the ten offenses against the Name / grieve like a child refusing to eat, [crying] even to an angry mother.
Being free from offenses, always practice the recitation of the Name; / through the Name alone, O divine sage, will everything of yours be accomplished, not otherwise.
Glorious Nārada said: / O Sanatkumāra, for those prone to reckless deeds, devoid of discernment and dispassion, / and devoted to the body, wealth, and ego, how can freedom from offenses arise for us?

Śrī Sanatkumāra said:
When an offence against the Name has occurred through heedlessness in any way,
one should constantly chant the Name, taking sole refuge in it.

For those beset by offences against the Name, the Names alone destroy the sin,
applied unceasingly, for they alone accomplish the objective.

A single name of his, being remembered or reaching the base of the ear, / whether pure or impure in syllables, uninterrupted, truly delivers [the soul].

If, however, it is thrown into greed and hypocrisy born of the body and wealth,
it does not produce its fruit quickly here, O brahmin.

This supreme secret, destroying all evil and averting offences,
was heard of old, O Nārada, from Śaṅkara.

The men engaged in offences who know the Name of Viṣṇu,
even for them there is liberation simply through reciting it, O Nārada.

The entire glorification of the Name is sung in the Purāṇa;
therefore, O giver of honor, you ought to hear the entire Purāṇa.

O brother, he who has faith every day in listening to the Purāṇa,
with him Śiva and Viṣṇu along with their followers become directly pleased.

The fruit one obtains having bathed at the holy site of Puṣkara, at Prayāga, or at the confluence with the sea—
double that fruit belongs to him who listens with faith.

Those who read the Purāṇas and attentively listen to them,
with every syllable they obtain the fruit born of the gift of a brown cow.

One without a son obtains a son; one seeking wealth obtains wealth;
one seeking knowledge obtains knowledge; one seeking liberation attains liberation.

Those who listen to the Purāṇas, having destroyed the web of sins
acquired across ten million births, indeed go to Hari's abode.

With a devotional disposition one should honor the brahmin Purāṇa-reciter
with cattle, land, gold, and garments, and with fragrant unguents and flowers, O sage,

and, full of joy, with a vessel made of bell-metal, a water pot,
earrings as well, and a signet ring made of gold.

So too one should give a seat and a flower garland, O ascetic;
one should not practice deceit regarding wealth, for [then] the gift bears inferior fruit.

A brahmin should cause the Purāṇa to be recited for the accomplishment of all desires and purposes,
[offering] gold, silver, cloth, a flower garland, and sandalwood.

Whoever gives the book with devotion goes to Hari's abode.
And those who complete the book according to this rule—
Citragupta does not write down their names, O twice-born.
